title: Adaptive client application-datagram batching architecture
purpose: Retain the proven low-pressure client UDP-segmentation mechanism while promoting a pressured connection back to the ordinary datagram representation without changing QUIC correctness ownership or the accepted listener batching path.
design_summary: Each built-in client connection owns one small adaptive batch policy shared by its runtime and endpoint host. New connections start eligible for the existing contiguous 1,472-byte application-datagram batch. At an existing flush boundary, the runtime counts distinct queued stream identifiers into a fixed twelve-entry stack buffer and stops at that bound. Repeated turns at the bound promote the policy one way for the connection lifetime; repeated writes for one stream remain sparse. After promotion the runtime stops renting contiguous batch owners and the endpoint disables UDP segmentation before using the ordinary per-datagram send path. Unsupported sockets never activate the batch observer, and a failed synchronous segmented submission falls back to ordinary individual sends. The connection actor remains the sole authority for queue mutation, packet construction, packet numbers, recovery, congestion and flow-control admission, path state, completion, cancellation, and disposal.
alternatives_considered: Enable client UDP segmentation unconditionally. Rejected by retained evidence because c1 and c4 improved while c16 tail latency and throughput credibly regressed.
Select on a fixed c16 or one-MiB benchmark shape. Rejected because benchmark identity is not a runtime pressure signal and would overfit the current harness.
Use raw queued-write count as the pressure signal. Rejected because one stream can own several queued write fragments and would be misclassified as multiplex pressure.
Demote back to segmentation as soon as pressure falls. Rejected because oscillation would complicate socket state, ownership, and evidence; the first policy uses one-way promotion.
Build a generic asynchronous sender queue. Rejected because the prior design accounted packets before delayed platform emission and failed dropped-FIN recovery.
edge_cases_and_constraints: A one-off queue burst must not promote the connection.
Once promoted, later sparse turns must not reactivate contiguous construction or UDP segmentation.
Promotion must not discard, reorder, duplicate, or re-account queued writes or protected packets.
Socket rebinding must reapply UDP segmentation only while the policy is still in the low-pressure state.

Path-specific packet-information sends, ECN or path changes, non-contiguous storage, partial packets, ACK-bearing packets, unsupported platforms, and custom send boundaries retain the individual-send fallback.
The listener/server batching path and public API remain unchanged.
data_and_state_considerations: The client adds one connection-local policy reference, one small consecutive-pressure counter, and one promoted flag. Pressure observation occurs once per queued-send flush, uses a fixed twelve-entry stack buffer, exits at the threshold, does not allocate, does not scan payloads, does not read wall-clock time, and does not retain stream identifiers. The endpoint and runtime share the same object only to coordinate representation and socket capability; it never owns packet or stream data.
risks: Distinct queued stream count remains a bounded proxy for multiplexing pressure; matched c1 through c32 evidence verifies that it preserves low-pressure gains without the unconditional high-pressure reversal.
Leaving UDP segmentation enabled after promotion could preserve platform overhead; the endpoint therefore disables the option before the promoted ordinary-send path.
A threshold below the existing batch capacity could penalize useful bursts; the first threshold is derived from the already bounded batch capacity and requires repetition.
Batch-observer dispatch could still add overhead after promotion; local high-pressure evidence must include the complete endpoint path rather than only policy microbenchmarks.
